item.title: Ackland Film Forum: "Set It Off" (F. Gary Gray, 1996) — Mon Oct 5, 7:30 PM — The Lumina Theater
item.description:
Jada Pinkett Smith, Queen Latifah, and Vivica A. Fox anchor this energetic reworking of the heist film. After a series of setbacks leaves four Black women with few viable paths forward, they embark on a string of increasingly audacious bank robberies. Blending humor, suspense, and tragedy, Set It Off captures both the bonds of friendship and the pressures of race, gender, and economic inequality in 1990s urban America. This film will be introduced by Professor Daelena Tinnin-Gadson, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event.

item.title: What AI Geeks Do for Fun: Mark Hinkle’s Multi-Model Playground — Tue Oct 6, 12:00 PM
item.description:
All Things AI (Live) A new series where people who are deep into AI show what they actually run, build, and tinker with when nobody’s making them.
First up: **Mark Hinkle** on multi-model workflows, homegrown agents, and the projects he vibe coded just to see if he could. So here’s the thing about AI talks. Most of them are either vendor demos or “10 prompts that will change your life.” This isn’t that.
**What AI Geeks Do for Fun** is a new series where practitioners open up their own setups and show the unpolished, “I built this on a Saturday” side of working with AI. What’s on their machines, which models they trust for what, what broke, and what they can’t stop playing with. I’m going first, because it’s only fair to embarrass myself before I ask anyone else to.
I’ll walk through:
* **My multi-model workflow.** Why I don’t pick one model. How I route work across Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and local open source models, and how they review each other’s work. * **How I build agents.**

This event is part of a series of workshops associated with the Día de los Muertos Ofrenda, installed at Duke Chapel from October 3 - November 2. Visitors can make contributions to this altar at any time.
This class introduces the student to the tradition of Dia de Muertos. Spanning over 3500 years, the class illuminates the major shifts in the development of this tradition and how it came to be what it is today. Class will address how to construct an ofrenda, and teach the student how to produce paper cempaxochitl (marigolds) and papel picado ( cut paper).
This workshop will be held in Spanish and English.
Please note, this workshop is held in the Crypt of Duke Chapel which is only accessible by stairs.

item.description:
At a time of rising antisemitism and deep cultural division, Tony Award-winning actor and activist Ari'el Stachel invites audiences into an exclusive intimate evening of performance, storytelling, and conversation.
This newly created work draws from Ari'el's own life and experiences, exploring themes that have long informed his work as an artist and advocate.
Through humor, vulnerability, and transformative character work, Ari'el explores Jewish identity, mental health, and belonging as an Arab-Jewish artist navigating multiple worlds.
Written and performed by Stachel, this new work explores his experiences with OCD, assimilation, and the complicated evolution of his Arab-Jewish identity. As a Middle Eastern Jewish teenager in America in the aftermath of 9/11, Ari'el quickly learned that safety often meant silence. item.description:
The National Association for self-esteem defines self-esteem as: “The experience of being capable of meeting life’s challenges and being worthy of happiness.” While this sounds remarkably simple, developing and maintaining healthy self-image is a challenging task. Poor self-image accounts for many problems that have greater impact upon adults. Starting young children on a path towards confidence in who they are and their abilities is vital, to increase the likelihood of a more satisfying, self-assured life for them as adults.

item.description:
When thinking about the future of AI, social work may not be the first field that comes to mind. However, researchers and educators at UNC’s School of Social Work have long been engaged in AI-related projects and have unique insights to share about how the technology can be used to address important social problems.
This panel discussion between School of Social Work faculty will explore current and potential uses of AI in social work research and education and key ethical considerations related to its use in the field. The panelists include experts with more than a decade of experience in AI-involved research as well as relatively recent adopters of the technology.
This is a hybrid event. Join us at https://unc.zoom.us/j/96298278191.

item.title: The Bettie Allison Rand Lectures in Art History: Alexander Marr, University of Cambridge — Tue Nov 3, 5:30 PM — Hyde Hall
item.description:
Pictorial Intelligence in Renaissance Art: Holbein’s Wit
The Renaissance witnessed intense debate about the nature and location of human intelligence. When it came to artists, this was focused on natural endowments versus trained skill, the relationship between the mind and the hand, and—especially among humanists—whether pictorial art was capable of intelligent authorship as opposed to mere replication of the visible world. Taking Hans Holbein the Younger as a case study, this lecture will explore how the mindful hand of a supremely gifted painter could demonstrate the inherent ingenuity and playful wit of an inventive--rather than merely mimetic--artistic intelligence.
Alexander Marr is University Professor of Renaissance and Early Modern Art. He specializes in European art 1400-1800, especially its intellectual and literary aspects in their social contexts. His most recent publication is Holbein's Wit: Pictorial Ingenuity in Renaissance Art.

item.title: Best Friend or Cybermother? A Confucian Reflection on AI Companionship — Tue Oct 6, 12:00 PM — Rubenstein Library Carpenter Conference Room 249
item.description:
AI companions designed to simulate romantic or friendly intimacy are rapidly expanding, but most critiques remain framed by Western liberal assumptions. I develop an alternative critique grounded in Confucian ethics. It begins by challenging the industry claim that AI companions offer a remedy for loneliness.
Against this view, I argue that Confucianism values positive solitude as a condition of self-cultivation and a precondition for genuine friendship. I further argue that AI companions are better understood as cyber mothers, inviting dependency and regression rather than ethical development. On this basis, I also criticize Nobel prize winner Geoffrey Hinton's proposal that future AGI should be designed to exhibit maternal love.
